title: Pass by Reference
description: Use & in a parameter so a function can change the caller's own variable.

content.value: When a Copy Is Not What You Want

items: A parameter is normally a copy. `score` in `main` never moved. Usually that is right, and returning is the clean way to send an answer back.
Sometimes changing the caller's variable **is** the job: swap two variables, update a running total, hand back two answers.
For those, a parameter can be a **reference** instead of a copy. It takes one character: `&`.

content.text: Call your friend Alexander "Alex" and it is still the same person. A reference is a second name for a variable that already exists.

content.caption: The two functions have identical bodies. The only difference is the `&` in `int& number`, and it changes everything.

content.question: What does `int& n` in a parameter list mean?
options: `n` is a copy of the argument
`n` is another name for the caller's variable
content.explain: The `&` makes `n` a reference: a second name for the variable passed in, so changes to `n` change it.

items.title: Pass by value
items.text: The function gets the value and keeps it to itself. The caller's variable is safe.

items.title: Pass by reference
items.text: The function gets the caller's variable itself. Changing `n` changes it.

content.title: Two ways to pass
content.caption: You can write `int& n` or `int &n`: both mean the same. This course keeps `&` against the type, because "int reference" is what it is.

steps.note: Call `changeIt`, passing `lives`. Because of `&`, no copy is made.
`other` is not a new box. It is a second name for `lives`.
Changing `other` changes the one shared box.
The function ended, so the name `other` is gone. The change it made stays.

content.title: Two names, one box
content.outro: The names do not have to match. `other` and `lives` are one box for as long as the call lasts.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `n` is a reference to `x`, so `n = 8` changes `x` itself.

content.value: `a = b; b = a;` cannot swap: the first line wipes out `a` before it is saved. You need a temporary third variable, `temp`, to hold one value for a moment.

items.title: Swaps the copies
items.text: The copies swap, then get thrown away. `main` prints `x = 1, y = 2`.

items.title: Swaps main's variables
items.text: `a` is `x` and `b` is `y`, so the swap happens to them.

steps.note: Pass both. With `&`, nothing is copied.
Back in `main`. `temp`, `a` and `b` are gone, and the swap stayed.

content.title: Watch the swap reach main
content.outro: No `return` could do this: a function returns one value, and a swap changes two.

content.question: Without `&`, what would `swapValues(x, y)` do to `x` and `y`?
content.explain: Plain parameters are copies. The copies get swapped, then thrown away when the function ends.

content.value: A `return` hands back one value. With references, the caller makes the variables and the function fills them in.

content.caption: `a` and `b` are only read, so they are plain. `quotient` and `remainder` are filled in, so they are references, often called **output parameters**. `q` and `r` start without values: safe, because `divide` always sets both.
The trackers live in `main` and every call updates them in place. The parameter list says exactly which of the caller's variables may change: the ones with `&`.

items.title: Does not compile
items.text: `cannot bind non-const lvalue reference of type 'int&' to an rvalue of type 'int'`: a value has nowhere to keep the change.

items.title: Compiles
items.text: A variable, so the change has somewhere to go.

content.title: A reference needs a real variable

content.question: Given `void addTenReal(int& n)`, which call compiles?
content.explain: A non-const reference must name a real variable. A plain value or a calculation has nowhere to store the change.

content.value: const References, and Which to Use

parts.label: read only
parts.note: The function promises not to change `text`. Trying to would not compile.

parts.label: reference
parts.note: No copy is made of the caller's string.

content.title: A read-only reference
content.caption: Passing a long `string` by value copies every character. A reference skips the copy, and `const` promises not to change it.
Because nothing is changed, a `const` reference also accepts a plain value like `"Functions"`. You will see `const string&` all over real C++ code.

items.sub: The default, for numbers and characters the function only reads.
When the function works out one answer.
Only when changing the caller's variable is the job, or for more than one answer.
For a string the function only reads.

content.value: A `&` parameter warns the reader: "this call may change your variable". Use it when you mean it, so the warning stays meaningful. Module 8 shows what is underneath: memory addresses and pointers.

quiz.question: What does the `&` in `void addTen(int& number)` do?
options: Makes number a copy of the caller's value
Makes number another name for the caller's variable, so changes reach it
Means the function returns two values
quiz.explain: That is pass by reference. Without the `&`, the function would only ever change its own copy.

quiz.question: After `int x = 1, y = 2;` and a call to `void swapValues(int& a, int& b)`, what are x and y?
quiz.explain: a and b were other names for x and y, so the swap happened to main's variables.

quiz.question: Why does `addTen(5)` fail when the parameter is `int& number`?
options: A reference must refer to a real variable, and 5 is just a value
Because references only work with strings
quiz.explain: There is nowhere to keep the change. Pass a variable instead.

quiz.question: Which is the best way for a function to hand back two answers, like a quotient and a remainder?
options: Two reference parameters that the function fills in
Print both and hope the caller reads them
quiz.explain: Only one `return` ever runs. Output parameters let the caller supply variables for the function to fill.

quiz.question: What does `const string& text` promise?
options: The string will be changed for the caller
The string is not copied, and the function will not change it
quiz.explain: A reference avoids the copy, and `const` forbids changes. It is the usual way to pass a string a function only reads.
